questions.prompt: Objective 1.1 covers decision criteria for choosing between two ways of structuring work. Which pair of approaches do those criteria compare?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK and agent loops
Self-hosted and Anthropic-hosted deployment
A fixed workflow and an autonomous agent

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the guide names exactly one decision axis (workflow versus agent); the two distractors are the other named pairings from objective 1.2, so each option tests a real boundary rather than padding. Two would have hidden the 1.1/1.2 boundary that makes the item worth asking.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that the Agent SDK and hand-rolled loops are the architecture decision; they are construction methods listed under 1.2, not the workflow-versus-agent choice.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between architectural choice and deployment choice; self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted is a managed deployment model under 1.2.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.1 (Agent Architecture) explicitly includes the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent as part of the architectural principles, patterns, and tradeoffs it measures.

whyWrong.a: The Claude Agent SDK and custom agent loops and harnesses are construction methods named under objective 1.2, not the architectural decision 1.1 describes.
whyWrong.c: Self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted is a managed agent deployment model named under objective 1.2, not the workflow-versus-agent architectural decision.

explanation.analogy: Architecture picks the shape of the solution (fixed steps or autonomous judgement); construction and deployment pick the machinery and where it runs.
explanation.takeaway: Objective 1.1 is about choosing between a workflow and an agent; the SDK, loops, and hosting models belong to objective 1.2.
explanation.deepDive: 1.1 is framed as architecture decisions rather than about the tools that build them, which is why the construction and pattern objectives keep turning up as distractors throughout Domain 1.

quotes: Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.

questions.prompt: A release pipeline needs a validation step that runs the same way every time, with no model deciding whether it happens. Which objective 1.2 mechanism fits?

options.text: Hooks, the mechanism named for deterministic actions
Agentic abstraction frameworks such as LangGraph
Sub-agents, listed among the common agent design patterns

Both distractors are named, real mechanisms rather than padding; a fourth would have repeated one of those layers.

distractorRationale.a: Probes choosing the framework layer because the pipeline has several stages; abstraction frameworks are named in 1.3 for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks, not for making a single action repeatable.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for a delegation pattern when the requirement is a fixed, repeatable step; sub-agents are a 1.3 design pattern, not a determinism mechanism.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.2 names hooks as the mechanism for deterministic actions, which matches a validation step that must run identically every time.

whyWrong.a: Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI are the agentic abstraction frameworks named under 1.3, used for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks. A framework organises multi-step work; it is not what makes one action run identically every time.
whyWrong.c: Sub-agents are listed among the common agent design patterns in objective 1.3. Delegating work to another agent still involves an agent deciding what to do, so it is not what makes a step deterministic.

explanation.takeaway: When an action must always happen the same way, the guide points to hooks.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 1.2 names exactly one mechanism for deterministic actions: hooks. Custom agent loops and harnesses are named in the same objective as construction methods, but the guide attaches no determinism claim to them, so a defensible answer has to be hooks.

questions.prompt: The guide says agentic abstraction frameworks are for building agents and workflows for a particular kind of task. Which kind?

Model selection experiments trading cost against quality

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the stated purpose, plus one option that denies any orchestration is needed and one that recasts framework choice as tuning work. Two would have reduced the multi-step qualifier to a single contrast, which is the part actually being tested.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that frameworks only matter for complicated work; the guide ties frameworks to multi-step tasks, which is the opposite of the no-orchestration case.

explanation.takeaway: Frameworks in 1.3 exist for multi-step tasks, which is exactly where single-call approaches stop being enough.
explanation.deepDive: Linking the framework layer back to the pattern list: tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, and context-window management are the patterns a framework helps you express for multi-step work.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.2 (Systems Life Cycle) covers systems life cycle management used to do what?

Develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems

distractorRationale.a: Probes substituting a design-build-deploy-retire delivery pipeline for the develop-implement-operate-maintain set the guide states.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing systems life cycle management with project management process groups.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing systems life cycle management with a product discovery and delivery framing.

whyWrong.c: Plan, analyze, control, and measure describes project management activities, which the guide does not name for 2.2.
whyWrong.d: Discover, define, deliver, and support is a product framing; the guide names lifecycle verbs applied to IT systems.

explanation.takeaway: Systems life cycle management in 2.2 means develop, implement, operate, and maintain.
explanation.deepDive: 2.2 is 2.8% of the exam, the smallest skill in Domain 2, and the guide gives it a single sentence. There is nothing further to study here beyond the four verbs and the fact that the object is IT systems.

questions.prompt: An operations team has inherited a system that is already in production and needs a framework for running it, fixing defects, and evolving it over its life. Which Domain 2 objective does that work sit under?

options.text: Objective 2.1, Understanding Requirements
Objective 2.4, Software Engineering Foundations
Objective 2.2, Systems Life Cycle

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the objective that owns life cycle management plus its two nearest Domain 2 neighbours. The three-way boundary is the whole point - 2.1 ends at requirements and 2.4 is engineering practice - so a fourth option would blur rather than sharpen the distinction.

distractorRationale.a: Probes swapping requirements work (2.1) for the operate and maintain half of life cycle work (2.2); a system already running in production has no requirements left to gather.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for 2.4 because code review and refactoring are what a team actually does to fix defects; those are engineering practices named inside 2.4, not a framework for managing a system across its life.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.2 covers systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks. Running, repairing, and evolving a system that has already shipped is the operate-and-maintain half of that scope.

whyWrong.a: 2.1 is Understanding Requirements, covering functional and infrastructure requirements based on business requirements and solution architecture. It sits upstream of building and says nothing about running a system afterwards.
whyWrong.c: 2.4 is Software Engineering Foundations, covering practices such as REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, SDLC integration, code review, and refactoring. Using those practices to fix defects is not the same work as managing the system across its life.

explanation.takeaway: Operating and maintaining a live system is still 2.2 - requirements are 2.1 and engineering practice is 2.4.
explanation.deepDive: The word 'operate' is the one candidates most often drop from their notes for 2.2, because it sounds like an IT-operations topic rather than an architectural one. It is inside the objective, and 2.4 does not cover it either: refactoring and code review are practices, not a framework applied across a system's life.

quotes: Systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks used to develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems.

questions.prompt: A research agent keeps appending raw tool output until its context is bloated and has drifted off the original task. Which techniques does Domain 6.1 name for this?

options.text: Tool output pruning and compaction
Token usage tracking and cost modeling
Few-shot examples and output constraints

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options so the item separates 6.1's context techniques from the cost and prompt techniques that look similar once a long-running agent starts misbehaving.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reaching for the cost vocabulary of 5.4. Usage tracking and cost modeling tell you what a run costs, not what to remove from the context.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the prompt-versus-context confusion. Examples and output constraints shape the instruction, while 6.1 manages what stays in the window.

explanation.correct: 6.1 names context window management and the prevention of context drift and bloat through tool output pruning and compaction as core context engineering techniques.

whyWrong.a: Token usage tracking and cost modeling belong to 5.4. They account for spend and do not stop a context from drifting or growing bloated.
whyWrong.c: Few-shot examples and output constraints are prompt engineering methods from 6.2. The 6.1 answer is pruning tool output and compacting the context.

explanation.takeaway: Context drift and bloat are fought with tool output pruning and compaction.

Context isolation through subagents or agentic workflows

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options for a clean structural distinction: 6.1 names isolation via subagents and multi-step workflows, and its opposite is the capacity misconception worth probing.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that more context capacity or more thinking effort isolates work. Neither creates the separation 6.1 describes.

explanation.correct: 6.1 names context isolation through subagents or multi-step agentic workflows as the technique for keeping parts of a task's context separate.

whyWrong.b: A larger context window holds more; it does not separate anything. Effort levels are a 5.1 model option. The isolation 6.1 names comes from subagents or multi-step workflows.

explanation.takeaway: Context isolation comes from subagents or multi-step agentic workflows, not from a bigger window.

quotes: Context and memory management techniques for Claude applications, including context window management, prevention of context drift and bloat (tool output pruning, compaction), and context isolation through subagents or multi-step agentic workflows.

questions.prompt: Which pair of items does Domain 6.2 list as prompt engineering methods?

options.text: Few-shot examples and input sanitization
Prompt caching and cost modeling
Subagents and multi-step agentic workflows

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the item tests recall of the 6.2 method list against the neighbouring technique lists from 5.4 and 6.1, which is the boundary most often crossed.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the prompt-versus-cost boundary. Prompt caching and cost modeling sit in 5.4 and target spend, not how a prompt is written.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the prompt-versus-context boundary. Subagents and multi-step agentic workflows sit in 6.1 and target how context is isolated, not the wording of the instruction.

explanation.correct: 6.2 lists instruction clarity, few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, prompt and instruction placement across components, iterative refinement, prompt adjustment, and input sanitization.

whyWrong.a: Prompt caching and cost modeling are cost techniques from 5.4. They reduce spend rather than improve how a prompt is written.
whyWrong.c: Subagents and multi-step agentic workflows are context isolation techniques from 6.1. They shape how much context a task carries, not how the instruction is worded.

explanation.takeaway: Prompt engineering is clarity, examples, placement, constraints, iteration, and sanitization.

source.section: 6.2 Prompt Engineering (cross-reference: 5.4 Cost and Token Management)
quotes: Prompt engineering principles and methods (instruction clarity, few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, prompt and instruction placement across components, iterative refinement, prompt adjustment, input sanitization) when writing and iterating on prompts for Claude.

questions.prompt: Only one of these appears in Domain 6.2's list of prompt engineering principles. Which one is it?

options.text: Response validation
Defensive parsing
Instruction clarity
Effort levels

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the item discriminates prompt-side, output-side, and model-side concerns at once, and each of the three distractors is a real technique named elsewhere in the guide.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the prompt-versus-output boundary. Response validation is a 6.3 output handling pattern, not a principle for writing the instruction.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the prompt-versus-output boundary on the consuming side. Defensive parsing is how output is read, not how a prompt is written.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the prompt-versus-model-option boundary. Effort levels are named under 5.1's model options.

explanation.correct: Instruction clarity appears in Domain 6.2's prompt engineering list, which also covers few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, prompt and instruction placement across components, iterative refinement, prompt adjustment, and input sanitization.

whyWrong.b: Response validation is named in Domain 6.3 as an output handling pattern. 6.2 lists principles for composing the request.
whyWrong.c: Defensive parsing is a Domain 6.3 output handling pattern for consuming responses. It does not belong in the prompt engineering list.
whyWrong.d: Effort levels appear in Domain 5.1 under model options. They are a model-level control, not a prompt engineering principle.

explanation.takeaway: Prompt engineering shapes what you send; output handling shapes what you do with what comes back.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 6.2 names eight principles and methods: instruction clarity, few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, prompt and instruction placement across components, iterative refinement, prompt adjustment, and input sanitization. The objective frames them as what applies when writing and iterating on prompts for Claude, but it ranks them not at all, groups them not at all, and defines none of them. Input sanitization sits in the same flat enumeration as the wording techniques rather than as a closing step, so treat the set as something to recall rather than a procedure to run.

questions.prompt: Which set does Domain 6.3 list for producing, validating, and consuming Claude output?

options.text: Instruction clarity, few-shot examples, input sanitization
Token budgeting, prompt caching, cache check-pointing
Structured output patterns, response validation, defensive parsing

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the item asks you to recognise the output handling cluster against the prompt-side and cost-side clusters that sit right beside it in the guide.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the output-versus-prompt boundary. These 6.2 methods shape the instruction sent to the model rather than how the response is produced and read.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the output-versus-cost boundary. Budgeting and caching are 5.4 techniques that manage spend, not response correctness.

explanation.correct: 6.3 covers producing, validating, and consuming output through structured output patterns, response validation, and defensive parsing, together with skepticism toward confident output.

whyWrong.a: Instruction clarity, few-shot examples, and input sanitization are Domain 6.2 prompt engineering methods. They affect what is sent, not how output is produced and read.
whyWrong.c: Token budgeting, prompt caching, and cache check-pointing are Domain 5.4 cost techniques. They control spend rather than output correctness.

explanation.takeaway: 6.3 output handling is structured output patterns, response validation, defensive parsing, and skepticism toward confident output.

questions.prompt: A response parses cleanly, sounds completely certain, and cites a plausible source. What does Domain 6.3 direct you to do next?

options.text: Stay skeptical — validate it defensively before relying on it
Ship it — confident, well-formed output is reliable by default

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options for a clean binary: objective 6.3 names skepticism toward confident output explicitly, and its opposite is the single misconception that phrase exists to counter.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating fluency and confidence as evidence of correctness, which is exactly the assumption 6.3's skepticism toward confident output is meant to counter.

explanation.correct: 6.3 includes skepticism toward confident output alongside structured output patterns, response validation, and defensive parsing, so confident, well-formed output still has to be validated before anything relies on it.

whyWrong.a: Confidence and clean formatting are not evidence of correctness. 6.3 asks you to validate and parse defensively even when the output sounds certain.

explanation.analogy: A confident witness is still only a witness — check the transcript before relying on the testimony.
explanation.takeaway: Confident output is still unverified output — validate it before you rely on it.

quotes: Established patterns and techniques for producing, validating, and consuming Claude output, including structured output patterns, response validation, defensive parsing, and skepticism toward confident output.

questions.prompt: Which set of topics does the Developer Foundations guide place under 7.1, AI Application Security?

Content policy, guardrail layering, and secure-by-design principles
Data privacy and security best practices, from prompt injection to PII handling

distractorRationale.a: Probes the common mistake of treating efficiency topics as security topics; objective 7.1 names none of them under AI Application Security.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between AI application security (7.1) and guardrails with secure-by-design (7.2); content policy, guardrail layering, identity and access management, and least privilege are all named under 7.2.

explanation.correct: 7.1 is data privacy and security best practices: prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, and PII handling.

whyWrong.a: Objective 7.1 covers prompt injection, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, PII handling, and the security properties to ensure. Routing, caching, and token budget management are not among the topics it names.
whyWrong.c: Content policy, guardrail layering, and secure-by-design principles (privacy, identity and access management, least privilege) are the two halves of 7.2, Guardrails and Safe Deployment.

explanation.takeaway: 7.1 is the data-privacy and application-security skill: injection, jailbreaks, untrusted input, leakage, and PII.
explanation.analogy: Think of 7.1 as the alarm system inside the building; 7.2 is the building policy and the way the doors are designed.

quotes: Data privacy and security best practices, including prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, PII handling, and ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

questions.prompt: A customer-support assistant will read free-text messages pasted in by end users. Which pair of concerns does 7.1 name as in scope for this?

options.text: Prompt injection awareness and mitigation, and jailbreak defense
Guardrail layering and content policy for safe deployment
Hooks that stop destructive actions inside Claude applications

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the 7.1 pair named in the guide, plus the two adjacent security mechanisms a candidate is most likely to grab instead. Both distractors are real skills in this domain, just wrong ones for this prompt.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the swap between detecting bad input (7.1) and controlling what the deployed system may output (7.2).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the swap between input-side defense (7.1) and the control named under 7.3, Claude Hooks.

explanation.correct: 7.1 explicitly names prompt injection awareness and mitigation and jailbreak defense, which is exactly the risk when untrusted user text reaches a Claude application.

whyWrong.b: Guardrail layering and content policy belong to 7.2's safe and responsible deployment practices; they shape deployment policy rather than defending the application against injection attempts in its input.
whyWrong.c: Hooks are named in 7.3 as a way to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications, which is a different control from defending the input path.

explanation.takeaway: Untrusted user text is a 7.1 problem: prompt injection awareness and mitigation, plus jailbreak defense.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 7.1 also lists untrusted input handling and data leakage prevention. The guide does not define how injection is detected or blocked, so do not expect mechanism-level detail.

quotes: Data privacy and security best practices, including prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, PII handling, and ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

questions.prompt: Which group of properties does 7.1 say a Claude application should ensure?

options.text: Latency, accuracy, and context capacity at inference time
Authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity
Availability, scalability, and cost efficiency once deployed

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the exact list from 7.1 plus two plausible-sounding non-security property groups that candidates might substitute from performance and cost reasoning.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between model-performance properties and the security properties 7.1 asks you to ensure.
distractorRationale.b: Probes reading availability and scalability as security requirements; objective 7.1 names confidentiality and integrity instead, and says nothing about operational efficiency here.

explanation.correct: 7.1 ends with ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity. Those five words are the recall target for the tail of the objective.

whyWrong.a: Latency, accuracy, and context capacity are model-selection and optimization concerns, not the security properties listed under 7.1.
whyWrong.b: Availability and scalability are operational concerns, and cost efficiency is a token-management topic; none appear in 7.1's list.

explanation.takeaway: The five properties 7.1 names are authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

quotes: Data privacy and security best practices, including prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, PII handling, and ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

questions.prompt: Which pair does the guide list as a secure-by-design principle under 7.2, Guardrails and Safe Deployment?

options.text: Jailbreak defense and untrusted input handling
Identity and access management, and least privilege

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options, because objective 7.2 draws a clean boundary: each side is a phrase the guide uses verbatim under one of the two objectives, so a third option would blur rather than sharpen the distinction being tested.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the most common mix-up in this domain: application-level defenses against hostile input (7.1) versus design-time access principles (7.2).

explanation.correct: 7.2 splits into two halves: safe and responsible deployment practices (content policy, guardrail layering) and secure-by-design principles, which objective 7.2 names as privacy, identity and access management, and least privilege.

whyWrong.b: Jailbreak defense and untrusted input handling are named under 7.1, AI Application Security. They defend the running application; 7.2's secure-by-design principles are privacy, identity and access management, and least privilege.

explanation.takeaway: Guardrails and deployment policy are 7.2; defenses against hostile input are 7.1.
explanation.deepDive: Both objectives appear in the same domain and both mention privacy. The reliable split is the emphasis: 7.1 is defending the application, 7.2 is the deployment and design posture.

quotes: Safe and responsible deployment practices (content policy, guardrail layering) and secure-by-design principles (privacy, identity and access management, least privilege).

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling application-security phrases into a question about deployment practice.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusion with the MCP communication patterns in 8.2, which a candidate may associate with 'deployment' generally.

explanation.correct: 7.2 names content policy and guardrail layering as its safe and responsible deployment practices, alongside secure-by-design principles.

whyWrong.a: Prompt injection awareness and data leakage prevention are named under 7.1, AI Application Security, not as deployment practices.
whyWrong.b: stdio, sockets, and client vs. server are the MCP communication patterns listed under 8.2, MCP Server Development.

explanation.takeaway: For 7.2 remember the pair: content policy and guardrail layering.

questions.prompt: According to the guide, what are Claude hooks for inside a Claude application?

options.text: Managing credentials and API keys across environments
Writing tool descriptions and handling errors when tools are called
Acting as guardrails and safety controls that block destructive actions

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: objective 7.3's own sentence plus the two neighbouring skills a candidate is likely to confuse it with, each of which is a real objective the guide defines elsewhere.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between hooks (7.3) and secret and credential management (7.4), which are adjacent items in the same domain.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between hooks (7.3) and tool implementation work in 8.1, where error handling and tool descriptions are named.

explanation.correct: Objective 7.3 is about leveraging hooks for guardrails and safety controls to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications.

whyWrong.a: Secrets, credentials, and API keys across development and production are the subject of 7.4, Identity, Secrets, and Key Management, not of hooks.
whyWrong.c: Tool description writing and error handling are named under 8.1, Tool Implementation. Hooks are described in terms of safety controls, not tool authoring.

explanation.takeaway: Hooks are the safety controls that prevent destructive actions inside a Claude application.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 7.3 gets a single sentence of detail: hooks are leveraged as guardrails and safety controls to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications. It names no hook events, payloads, or configuration syntax, so do not expect mechanism-level detail.

questions.prompt: Objective 7.4 names three specific activities alongside managing secrets, credentials, and API keys. Which pair is on that list?

options.text: Secure-by-design access controls and least privilege
Access approval and level verification, plus monitoring
Data privacy and PII handling, plus leakage prevention

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the item discriminates 7.4's own three sub-clauses against the two neighbouring objectives whose wording is easiest to borrow — 7.2's access language and 7.1's privacy language. The options are deliberately the same shape and length, so the objective boundary is the only clue.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the nearest near-miss in the domain: an access-control phrase is close, but 7.2 states these as secure-by-design principles rather than as one of 7.4's three sub-clauses.
distractorRationale.c: Probes borrowing the data privacy half of 7.1's scope, which is application security rather than credential and access management.

explanation.correct: 7.4 names access approval and level verification along with authorized access monitoring, as two of the three activities it covers alongside managing secrets, credentials, and API keys.

whyWrong.a: Access controls and least privilege are named, but as secure-by-design principles under 7.2, Guardrails and Safe Deployment. 7.4's three sub-clauses are identity validation and authentication, access approval and level verification, and authorized access monitoring.
whyWrong.c: Data privacy and PII handling with data leakage prevention belongs to 7.1, AI Application Security. Protecting the data an application processes is not the same work as approving an access level and watching that authorized access.

explanation.takeaway: 7.4 covers approving access and verifying the level granted, together with monitoring that the access stays within bounds.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 7.4 treats access as a lifecycle, not a single step: who you are, what you are cleared for, and then watching that the clearance is used. The guide names the three activities but gives no procedure for any of them.

The resources, tools, and prompts option earns its place because it is genuinely 8.2 content, so the item tests the label the guide attaches rather than the objective the content comes from.

distractorRationale.b: Probes swapping the 8.1 tool usage patterns into a question about MCP communication, which is the exact confusion the two labelled lists are designed to prevent.
distractorRationale.c: Probes stopping at the objective boundary instead of the label: resources, tools, and prompts are named in the same 8.2 sentence, but the guide attaches the words 'communication patterns' only to stdio, sockets, and client versus server.

explanation.correct: Objective 8.2 names the communication patterns as stdio, sockets, and the client versus server distinction, alongside server authoring, deployment, integration, and the MCP resources, tools, and prompts.

whyWrong.b: Agentic harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, and approval patterns are the tool usage patterns listed under 8.1, Tool Implementation, not MCP communication patterns.
whyWrong.c: Resources, tools, and prompts are named in objective 8.2, so this set is in the right place — but the guide never labels them as communication patterns. That label belongs only to stdio, sockets, and client versus server.

explanation.takeaway: stdio, sockets, and client vs. server are the MCP communication patterns; the harness dispatch trio belongs to tool implementation.

quotes: MCP server development practices, including server authoring, deployment, integration with Claude applications, MCP resources, tools, and prompts, and communication patterns (stdio, sockets, client vs. server).

questions.prompt: You must choose between a built-in Tool, a custom Tool, a Skill, and an MCP. What does 8.3, Agentic Customization, tell you to do?

options.text: Weigh the tradeoffs among those options and apply the one that fits the use case
Author and deploy an MCP server, then integrate it with the application

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because objective 8.3 states a single tradeoffs decision among four named approaches; the distractor substitutes the execution steps of 8.2, and a third option would have to invent a rule the guide does not give.

distractorRationale.a: Probes jumping straight to the server-authoring workflow of 8.2 when 8.3 asks for a choice between approaches, and for an unwarranted default of always building a server.

explanation.correct: 8.3 is the selection objective: weigh the tradeoffs among the available options and apply whichever fits the given use case.

whyWrong.a: Authoring and deploying a server is the 8.2 skill. 8.3 is about the decision itself, and the guide gives no rule that picks one of the four approaches by default.

explanation.takeaway: 8.3 is a choice, not a construction step: weigh the tradeoffs among the options and pick the one that fits.
explanation.deepDive: The guide names the four options but does not define Skills or describe when each wins, so expect to be tested on recognising the four-way tradeoffs rather than on a decision table.

quotes: Tradeoffs among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs for selecting and applying the appropriate approach for a given use case.

Built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs
Tools, Agents, MCP servers, and vector stores

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options of nearly identical shape: the guide's exact four-item list, plus two plausible groups mixing in Security and Safety or agent-architecture vocabulary that the guide never puts into this comparison.

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling Security and Safety vocabulary into the customization choice, which is about capability mechanisms, not controls.
distractorRationale.c: Probes substituting Agent Architecture vocabulary for the actual four options; vector stores are not named in 8.3.

explanation.correct: 8.3 compares built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs. Those four names are the recall target.

whyWrong.a: Models is a model-selection concern, not a customization option; Guardrails, Hooks, and Secrets belong to Domain 7, Security and Safety. Neither is part of the tradeoff 8.3 names.
whyWrong.c: Neither Agents nor vector stores is among the four options 8.3 names; 8.3 names built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs.

explanation.takeaway: The 8.3 menu is exactly four items: built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs.
